cur:monumental-tokali-entry.summary: In a narrative frieze against a blue ground, Christ, haloed and inscribed IC XC, rides a white donkey towards the gate of a city at the right, where a crowd waits, while a figure in a tree above watches and another spreads a garment before him. The strip-like composition with Greek captions is typical of the long Gospel cycles of Cappadocian churches.
facts: Tokalı Kilise ('Church of the Buckle'), the largest church at Göreme, comprises an Old Church of the 10th century, painted in strips of red and green, and a larger New Church of the late 10th or early 11th century whose walls are dominated by rich indigo blue made from lapis lazuli.
The scene is captioned BAIOPHOROS, the Greek name of the Palm Sunday feast; the figure in the tree cutting branches follows Matthew 21:8.

cur:monumental-tokali-entry.notes: Some have read the figure in the tree as Zacchaeus and the scene as Christ entering Jericho, but the Greek caption BAIOPHOROS (Palm Sunday), visible in the companion photograph of this frieze, confirms the Entry into Jerusalem. The photograph shows a detail of the wall; whether the scene belongs to the Old or the New Church is not stated in the source. Dates for both phases are debated (c. 910s–920s for the Old Church; mid-10th to early 11th century for the New).

cur:objects-sinai-saint-peter-icon.summary: The apostle Peter stands in a gold halo, holding the keys of the Kingdom and a staff topped by a cross, his weathered face turned slightly toward the viewer. Above him, in three medallions, appear Christ at the centre with the Virgin and St John at the sides. The arrangement, recalling the portraits of officials on consular diptychs, presents Peter as the servant of the Lord who presides over him from heaven.
facts: Wikipedia describes it as a sixth-century encaustic icon, one of the oldest surviving icons of St Peter; above his head is a Deesis-like row of half-figures in medallions with Christ, the Virgin and John the Evangelist.
It survived Iconoclasm because Saint Catherine's Monastery lay outside the reach of the iconoclast emperors (context of the Sinai icons).
cur:objects-sinai-saint-peter-icon.notes: Dated 6th century by Wikipedia; the Commons file metadata gives 7th century.
